description: The house wakes up. Commands, the first eight verbs in three tenses, and the first ten letters.
objectives: Understand and give the commands of a morning: wake up, get up, come, go, sit, wait, look, eat.
Conjugate eight verbs in present, past, and command, with negatives, for all six persons.
Hear the difference between ā and a, kh and h, and written and spoken forms.
Read and write 10 letters (ا آ ب پ ت ث ن ی د ر و) and about 25 real words made from them.
Whisper your first gossip to Mass, and teach the girls “Bābā mige.”

words.root: From the old verb khastan, “to wound.” Tired is, literally, wounded.
sobh (morning) + -āne, the suffix of belonging: the morning thing. Spoken Tehrani turns ān into un.

example.en: Do you want a little tea?

words.root: do (two) + bār (a time). A second time.
khosh (good) + hāl (state, condition). The same hāl as in hālet chetore, “how is your state?”
nā- (not) + rāhat (at ease). Not at ease.
From the Arabic word for a bird’s crop, the pouch that holds its food. Your hosele is how much you can hold.
be- + bin, the present stem of didan (to see). The same bin as durbin, the “far-seer” (camera).
negāh (a look) + kon (do!). Do a look.

days.subtitle: Come and go: the first two verbs of every morning
days.objective: Understand Mass’s wake-up commands, conjugate come and go in three tenses, and read your first word: آب.

steps.title: Warm-up: what do you remember?
steps.instruction: Every lesson opens by pulling old words out of memory. Getting some wrong is how the remembering gets stronger.

steps.title: Listen first
steps.instruction: It’s 7 a.m. Sam is still in bed. Mass is already up. Play the scene twice before you look at the words. The English is hidden: tap a line to reveal it.

steps.title: New words
steps.instruction: Five words from the scene. Tap to hear each one, say it out loud, and read the small story under the words that have one.

steps.title: Verb lab: come and go
steps.intro: This week’s focus is the command (biyā! boro!), but a verb only makes sense once you see its whole life. Every Persian verb has two stems: one for the past and one for the present. The endings stay the same everywhere: -am (I), -i (you), -e (he/she), -im (we), -in (you, polite or plural), -an (they). In the tables, the prefix is coral, the stem is blue, and the ending is green. Tap any form to hear it.

steps.title: Ear gym: ā or a?
steps.instruction: Persian has a long, open ā (like “father”) and a short a (like “cat”). They change meaning. Listen to each pair until you can hear the difference, then take the test. Two voices speak, because hearing many voices trains the ear faster.

steps.title: Reading: ا آ ب پ

letters.name: alef
letters.sound: ā in the middle or end of a word; at the very start it carries a short vowel (a, e, o)
letters.tip: One stroke, top to bottom. Alef never joins the letter after it, so there’s always a little gap to its left.

letters.name: alef madde
letters.sound: ā at the start of a word
letters.tip: Alef with a wavy hat (madde, “stretch”). The hat stretches the start of a word into a long ā: āb, āre, āghā.

letters.name: be
letters.tip: A shallow boat, written right to left, then one dot underneath. Joined up, it shrinks to a small tooth with a dot below.

letters.name: pe
letters.tip: The same boat as be, with three dots below. Arabic has no p sound, so Persian added the dots to make one. It’s a Persian letter.

steps.intro: Persian runs right to left, and most letters hold hands with the next one, so each letter has up to four shapes: alone, at the start, in the middle, and at the end. The good news is that the shape barely changes. What changes are the dots. Learn letters in families: sound first, then shape, then name.

steps.title: Shadow Mass
steps.instruction: Play a line, then say it right on top of the voice, matching the rhythm and melody. Record yourself and compare. Shadowing trains your mouth and your ear together.

questions.prompt: Mass calls you from the kitchen. You’re on your way. What do you shout?
questions.explain: Persian says “I came!” while it’s still coming.

questions.prompt: Type what you hear, in English letters.

steps.title: In your notebook
tasks: Persian books open from what you’d call the back. Flip your notebook over and start on the right-hand page. This notebook is now Persian.
Write ا, آ, ب, and پ five times each, right to left, saying the sound every time: ā… b… p…
Write آب (āb), بابا (bābā), and پا (pā) three times each. Under each one, write the phonetics and the meaning.
Copy the past tense of raftan (go) from the verb lab, in phonetics: raftam, rafti, raft… Then cover it and write it again from memory.
On a page at the back, start a list called “Verbs I own.” Add umadan and raftan with both stems.

steps.title: Talk with Mass

openers.en: Good morning! Did you wake up?

steps.massNote: Sam is practicing come and go. When you call him, make him answer “umadam!”

steps.title: Teach the girls: Bābā mige
steps.game: Simon Says, Persian style. “Bābā mige…” means “Dad says…”. Call a command and they do it, but only if you said “Bābā mige” first. Older kids can take a turn calling the commands to catch you out.

days.subtitle: Sit, wait, get up, wake up: the verb that becomes
days.objective: Follow a breakfast exchange, see how one helper verb builds “get up” and “wake up,” and read بیا and نان.

steps.title: Warm-up: what do you remember?
steps.instruction: Yesterday’s words and some old friends from Mango.

steps.title: Listen first
steps.instruction: Breakfast. Listen twice, then tap lines for the English.

lines.en: Is there bread and cheese too?
lines.speaker: Sam

steps.title: New words
steps.instruction: Five words for the table.

steps.title: Verb lab: become and sit
steps.intro: shodan means “to become,” and it’s the engine behind half of yesterday’s words. Put an adjective in front and only shodan conjugates: boland (tall) + shodan = get up; bidār (awake) + shodan = wake up. Switch between them with the tabs and watch only the second word change. In these compounds the command drops its be-: boland sho, not boland besho.

steps.title: Ear gym: kh or h?
steps.instruction: Persian kh (خ) is a scrape at the back of the throat, like the ch in Bach. Plain h (ح or ه) is just breath. Mass’s “hālet chetore” starts with breath, not a scrape.

steps.title: Reading: ت ث ن ی

letters.name: te
letters.tip: The boat again, with two dots on top. Below means b or p; above means t, s, or n.

letters.name: se
letters.tip: Three dots on top. It sounds exactly like s and shows up only in words borrowed from Arabic, like masalan (for example). Learn to recognize it; you’ll rarely write it.

letters.name: nun
letters.tip: One dot on top. At the end of a word it becomes a deep bowl that dips below the line. In the middle it looks like be with the dot moved upstairs.

letters.name: ye
letters.sound: y, or the vowel i (and ey at the end of some words)
letters.tip: Two dots below while it’s joining; at the end of a word the Persian ye drops its dots and curls back like a swan. It writes the long i in bidār and biyā.

steps.intro: Four letters that share be’s boat. The dots tell them apart: two on top for t, three on top for s, one on top for n. Ye is the shape-shifter: it’s y, it’s the long i, and at the end of a word it loses its dots. Short vowels (a, e, o) usually aren’t written at all. You supply them from memory of the word, and as a speaker you already have that memory.
steps.aside: نی (ney) is the reed flute, the first image of Rumi’s Masnavi: “Listen to this reed, how it complains.” You can already read the word that starts the most famous poem in the language.

steps.title: Shadow Mass
steps.instruction: Match her rhythm. Record, compare, repeat.

questions.prompt: Mass has set the table. Which line means “Come sit”?
Type what you hear, in English letters.

steps.title: In your notebook
tasks: Write ت, ث, ن, and ی five times each in all their shapes. Say the sound every time.
Write بیا, نان, آبی, and نی. Under each: phonetics and meaning.
Draw a two-column table: “boland misham / boland shodam,” all six persons, from memory. Check it against the verb lab.
Add shodan and neshastan to “Verbs I own.” Note the collision: nashin = “don’t sit” and “don’t become.”

steps.title: Talk with Mass

openers.en: What are you having for breakfast?

steps.massNote: Sam is learning sit, wait, and again. When he says something, ask him to say it again: “dobāre begu!”

days.subtitle: Be and do: feelings, and the verb that builds verbs
days.objective: Say how you feel with the hidden “be” endings, use kardan to wait and hurry, and read بیدار and برو on your own.

steps.title: Warm-up: what do you remember?
steps.instruction: Retrieval first, always.

steps.title: Listen first
steps.instruction: A morning check-in. Listen twice before reading.

lines.en: I’m fine, but I’m tired. How are you?
lines.speaker: Mass

lines.en: I’m not upset. I’m just not in the mood.
lines.speaker: Mass

steps.title: New words
steps.instruction: Six words for how you feel.

steps.title: Verb lab: be and do
steps.intro: budan (to be) hides in the present: the endings alone carry it. Khub (fine) + am = khubam, I’m fine. After a word ending in a vowel, like khaste, the endings sit apart: khaste-am. In the negative, “be” borrows its own word: nistam, I’m not. kardan (to do) is the Lego verb: patience + do = wait; haste + do = hurry; a look + do = look.

steps.title: Ear gym: written vs. spoken
steps.instruction: Why does Mass say khune when the dictionary says khāne? Spoken Tehrani follows rules, and once you know them, her speech stops sounding like a different language from the textbook.

rules.name: ān → un
rules.text: A long ā before n becomes u.

rules.name: verbs shrink
rules.text: Written -ad becomes -e, -id becomes -in, -and becomes -an, and stems get squeezed.

steps.title: Reading: د ر و (the letters that never join forward)

letters.name: dāl
letters.tip: A bent elbow sitting on the line. Like alef, it never joins the letter after it.

letters.name: re
letters.sound: r (lightly tapped, like the tt in Spanish “pero”)
letters.tip: A short slide that dips below the line. Never joins forward. Next week, dots turn it into z (ز) and zh (ژ).

letters.name: vāv
letters.sound: v, or the vowels u and o
letters.tip: A small loop with a tail below the line. It writes v in vaght, u in nun, o in boro and to. Never joins forward.

steps.intro: Seven Persian letters refuse to join the letter after them: ا د ذ ر ز ژ و. You’ve met four. After one of them, the next letter starts fresh, which is why بیدار has a gap after the alef. With these three, a lot of your vocabulary suddenly becomes readable.
steps.aside: Two phrases you can now read and use at the front door: بیا تو (biyā tu, come in!) and برو بیرون (boro birun, go outside!).

steps.title: Shadow Mass
steps.instruction: Feelings carry melody. Copy her tune, not just her words.

lines.en: I’m fine, but I’m tired. How are you?
lines.speaker: Mass

lines.en: I’m not upset. I’m just not in the mood.
lines.speaker: Mass

questions.prompt: How do you say “I’m not upset”?
Type what you hear, in English letters.

steps.title: In your notebook
tasks: Write د, ر, and و five times each. Then write all 10 letters from this week in a row, from memory.
Write these words in script, with phonetics and meaning under each: بیدار، برو، دیر، پنیر، نون، بیرون، دوربین.
Write a feelings table in phonetics: khaste-am, khaste-i, khastas… then the same for khoshhāl.
Write three true sentences about how you feel today, in phonetics. Read them to Mass.

steps.title: Talk with Mass
steps.massNote: Sam is learning to say how he feels (khaste-am, khoshhālam). Ask him how he is, and make him answer in full.

days.subtitle: Story day: see and eat, the first gossip, and a line of Hafez
days.objective: Follow a short story, gossip quietly with Mass, and read a line of Hafez with a word-by-word key.

steps.title: Warm-up: what do you remember?
steps.instruction: Mixed: this week and older words.

steps.title: Story, episode 1: The neighbor
steps.instruction: Sam and Massoumeh, by the window, every episode. Listen to the whole episode before reading. Then read along line by line.

lines.fa: صبحه. سام و معصومه تو خونه‌ان.
lines.en: It’s morning. Sam and Massoumeh are at home.
Yes. Every day he leaves late.
lines.speaker: Mass

questions.prompt: What does Mass tell Sam when he turns to look?
Sam thinks the man is tired. What does Mass think?

steps.title: New words
steps.instruction: Two ways to say look, plus the review words the story leans on.

steps.title: Verb lab: see and eat
steps.intro: didan (to see) has one of the most useful present stems in the language: bin. khordan (to eat) covers drinking too: Persians eat their tea. Use the tabs to try khordan with breakfast and with tea, and notice that the command keeps its bo- here.

steps.title: Gossip kit, part 1
steps.intro: Your dream is to hold a whispered conversation with Mass in public. It starts with eight phrases, almost all of them commands you now know how to build.

proverb.fa: دیوار موش داره، موش هم گوش داره.
proverb.tr: divār mush dāre, mush ham gush dāre.
proverb.en: The wall has mice, and the mice have ears.

steps.tip: Assume the person at the next table speaks Persian. Tehranis are everywhere.

steps.title: A line of Hafez

lines.fa: صبح است ساقیا قدحی پر شراب کن
lines.tr: sobh ast sāghiyā ghadahi por sharāb kon
lines.en: It’s morning, cupbearer: fill a cup with wine.

lines.fa: دور فلک درنگ ندارد شتاب کن
lines.tr: dowr-e falak derang nadārad shetāb kon
lines.en: The turning sky won’t linger. Hurry.

steps.note: Both halves end on kon, the same command as in sabr kon. Hafez gives two orders: fill the cup, and hurry. Iranians open his book at random for a fortune (fāl-e Hafez), above all on Yalda night, December 21. You’ll do that in Chapter 5.

items.story: A far-seer. Originally binoculars, now any camera.
Someone who sees bad. It also means suspicious, as in suspicious of your neighbors.

questions.prompt: In Hafez’s line, kon is the same verb as in…

steps.title: In your notebook
tasks: Copy Hafez’s couplet in phonetics, with the English under it. Underline both kon.
Start a page at the back called “Word stories.” Add durbin, khoshbin, badbin, and the words with a story from this week (khaste, sobhune, dobāre, khoshhāl, nārāhat).
Write the gossip kit in phonetics. Pick your three favorites and mark them for this weekend.
In script, write دوربین and بیرون. You can write every letter in them.

steps.title: Talk with Mass
steps.massNote: Sam is learning to gossip. Point at someone on TV or out the window and whisper about them in Farsi.

days.subtitle: Review day: all eight verbs, all ten letters, and the ham- family
days.objective: Conjugate eight verbs on demand, read six phrases with no help, and plan the weekend with Mass.

steps.title: Warm-up: the whole week
steps.instruction: Ten words from this chapter, shuffled.

steps.title: Ear gym: mixed review
steps.instruction: Every pair from this week, shuffled together. Mixing them is harder, and harder is better for memory.

steps.title: Verb gym: all eight verbs
steps.instruction: Random persons, tenses, and verbs, including negatives. It isn’t meant to be easy. A wrong answer shows you the right one.

steps.title: Secret messages
steps.instruction: Every letter in these phrases is one you learned this week. Read each one out loud, then tap to check.

steps.title: Word stories: the ham- family
steps.intro: You described hamsar as “other head.” It’s closer to “same head”: ham means same, together, or shared.

items.story: One who shares your head, usually glossed as sharing a pillow. Massoumeh is your hamsar.
The people who share your shade. Like the lazy man in the story.
One who shares your road. Iranians call a cell phone a “mobile” or a telefon-e hamrāh, the phone that travels with you.

steps.title: In your notebook
tasks: From memory, write all 10 letters in every shape they take. Then check.
Write the six secret messages in script, then the phonetics under each.
Fill one page with a verb chart from memory: raftan, umadan, didan, and khordan in the past tense, all six persons.
Write five sentences about your morning in phonetics. Use at least three different verbs and one negative.
Add the ham- family to “Word stories.”

steps.title: Talk with Mass

openers.en: What did you have for breakfast?

steps.massNote: Sam has learned the past tense of eight verbs. Ask him what he did today, and push for full sentences.

steps.title: Teach the girls: a morning routine
steps.game: Pick one line a day and use it every morning this week. Routines beat lessons with kids. By Friday it’s just how mornings sound.

steps.title: Optional: Mass’s voice
steps.instruction: The computer voices are clear but tidy. Real speech is faster and messier, and the fastest way to train your ear is many real voices. If Mass is willing, ask her to record these on her phone at her normal speed. Listen to them on walks.

weekendCards.massNote: Sam knows the present tense also means the near future: “fardā mirim” = we’ll go tomorrow. Make plans with him in Farsi.
Go somewhere public: a café, a grocery store, a park. Sam wants to whisper about people in Farsi. Keep it kind… or don’t.
